I hope this is the right subreddit for this. I posted it here because it's a question that can be answered by anyone who accepts the Bible as reflecting, in some way, the truth.

I should make the disclaimer that I'm not religious and haven't been for a very long time, and I don't believe in a god. But I think religious thought can be valuable and it fascinates me. I don't intend to start a debate. I just want to know what you all think about my thoughts on the Bible as literal Truth.

I come from the central United States. Where I'm from, a somewhat large and very vocal group of the population, of which my parents are part, are Christians who are creationists because they are what I would call Biblical literalists. Even when I was a Christian, I found this odd. I don't understand why the Bible must be literal for it to be true. If the Bible expresses a fundamental truth about the universe, I wouldn't be surprised if that truth is too profound to be expressed in literal terms—especially if the purpose was to be a universal spiritual beacon to those who would read it, rather than a text incomprehensible for humans.

In fact, I don't even think it's a threat to belief to hold that the entire Bible is metaphorical. That, even when it describes historical events, they are embellished or perhaps fabricated entirely to drive home a particular point. For Christians, does it really matter that Jesus physically died on a Roman cross, or is the point really the sacrificial and selfless ethic—the love—that his life and death represent? Must the prime article of faith be that Jesus rose from the grave, or could the more fundamental point be that the physical body is not all that exists, and that what is necessary is faith in God and his universal love? (From my meager understanding, this view would be less problematic for Muslims than for Christians.)

Of course, this interpretation has the added advantage of short-circuiting any criticisms of the Bible based on historical inaccuracy or internal contradiction. But that's not really my point. My point is that Christianity (also Islam, actually), it seems to me, is a religion of universality. The point of it all, in the end, is the universalization of the Church expressed in Paul's epistles. For Paul, whether you are a member of the Body of Christ is not subject to your place of origin, race, gender, etc.—not on whether you are Jew or Gentile—it is only a matter of whether you make the leap of faith, accept the Holy Ghost.

I don't have any answers, and this honestly might just be a shower thought. But I thought I'd post it and see what sort of feedback I get.

One problem a lot of Atheists have with the Bible is that no matter if you take it literally or metaphorically, it is riddled with contradictions and passages that are quite obviously morally wrong.

I'm not saying that there isn't truth in the Bible, it certainly contains statements that are true but they aren't true simply because they are in the Bible. There are statements and passages that can be objectively evaluated as being true.
Similarly it contains objectively good moral values and it contains objectively bad moral values.

Do not kill
Do not steal
These are objectively good morals, they are not good simply because they reside in the Bible.

The Bible is absolutely a valuable resource in a literary sense, but not much more.

The case for Biblical literallism.

The basic premise of Christianity is that mankind is sinful and needs to be reconciled to God. This is the building block the rest of Christianity is built on, so let's start there. Sin was brought into the world by mankind. Death is a result of sin. From here, we can see the importance of the Creation story being literal. If there was billions of years of living and dying before mankind was even on the scene, there is no premise for Christianity to be built on. So from the very beginning, the validity of the Bible is based on it being literal.

As far as Jesus dying on an actual Roman cross, it did not literally need to be that. An all powerful God could have chosen some other equally terrible death, but death on a Roman cross is what we got. All of the prophecies leading up to Christ point to death on a cross.

Now, while this is a thought out approach to it, there are also plenty of people who will say, "Teh B1ble is literal because God says so." They have put no thought into it. This can certainly be annoying.

Hi all,

Writing has been a favorite hobby of mine ever since I was young. I am a pre-law undergrad student currently, and am trying to think ahead and prepare for when I will have to apply to grad school, whether it be law school or something else. I have to admit that I don't have much in extracurriculars that I can put down on applications and I figured that I should finally use what has always been my favorite past time to supplement this. I have a simple idea that I think I could really have fun writing and illustrating, but the publishing and self-publishing processes are really confusing me. While my intention is not for this book to blow up and become a money-making sensation, I want it to have some success and go through a legitimate publishing house. On the other hand, self-publishing seems viable for my purposes. I guess my first question would be whether I should take the route of self-publishing or if I should take the time to find a publishing company that will look at my proposal/completed manuscript. It is my understanding that some will not consider unsolicited manuscripts but will look at unsolicited proposals. I am a college student so I am not willing to spend a great deal of money for either process, and hopefully that will not cause problems later down the road.

Thanks for your input!
Would like some input on the best way to go about making my idea for a children's book into something tangible.

You are putting the cart before the horse. Don't even think about those things until the work is done and you've had it professionally edited at least once. As to spending money, publishing is not something that should cost you money. Vanity presses will take your money and you won't have any success because there is no investment in it for them - you've given them the cash upfront. Got to writing/writers' festivals, join a writing group, network. Otherwise, without a manuscript in hand people aren't interested in talking theoretically, there are hundreds and thousands of people who HAVE got the manuscript in hand and they are going to get more interest than someone with just an idea.

So you definitely think that I should go through a publisher? As for actually having the manuscript, I agree completely with what you've already explained. I don't intend on contacting any publisher until I can provide a polished project.

Why don't you try writing and laying out your book first? Free programs like Apache Open Office let you create PDFs so they can be printed by self-publishers like Lulu.com or something. I published a private HC (hardcover) book there and it's not all that bad. You want a "legit" publisher only if you can't network for shit (and have essentially, no distribution network).

Awesome. I actually use Open Office for pretty much everything. I've read a little about Lulu, but I am concerned that I don't have any networking skills and I will be left with a book that nobody wants! :'( How bad were any fees that you had to pay? And you said that you published a "private" hardcover? What exactly do you mean by this? I will check out Lulu, though. Thanks!

Well, Lulu.com will take a percentage of your book sales (per item sold) if you decide to sell through them (printing costs, shipping costs, etc.). You have to do some arithmetic to see how you can get profitable.

Remember - publicity and sales/selling are different animals. As for book covers, you will have to do your own illustrations or commission an artist (that is appropriate) for your book/subject matter.

It depends, there are a few authors I know of who have gained publishing contracts after being self published, BUT, and it's a big one, they have usually had extensive PR or Marketing experience or are married to someone who does.

Definitely get a polished manuscript, BUT (sorry!) it's a case of fully expecting it to come back with some parts that have been altered or with requests to be altered in either flow or editing. There are some publishing houses who take unsolicited manuscripts, usually it's during one day/week/month of the year, I'd recommend having a look in book shop for publishers of books that yours would be like, and doing some searching online as to whether they do, how they'd like it submitted. Some (places/agents/editors) ask for it to be printed, others emailed, others on a USB, others as a PDF... The more research you can sort out in your down time, the better off you will be. If you do decide to follow through, I'd love to see some of your writing - as one writer and hopeful to another :) Best of luck, I hope I haven't scared you out of it. Just be brave with it and see where it takes you :)

Oh no! You are not scaring me at all. I do want to continue with writing, even if it necessarily isn't my career. I think that learning the steps of publishing will all come with time if I just keep at it. It sounds like I just need to take the time to look at specific publishers and learn about their requirements. As for the publisher making changes, I think I would just be happy I didn't receive a rejection letter! Haha. Thank you so much for your advice.

As to spending money, publishing is not something that should cost you money. Vanity presses will take your money and you won't have any success because there is no investment in it for them - you've given them the cash upfront. Got to writing/writers' festivals, join a writing group, network. Otherwise, without a manuscript in hand people aren't interested in talking theoretically, there are hundreds and thousands of people who HAVE got the manuscript in hand and they are going to get more interest than someone with just an idea.

A proposal is very different to "hey I have this idea" - it is usually the first chapter or 10% of a manuscript, with chapter breakdowns, an overview, an author statement. They are faster to assess, but have to be worth the read.

A good story shouldn't need money to get published.
